questions.question: How does binary search work and what is its time complexity?
questions.title: Binary Search Algorithm Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Binary search works on a sorted array by repeatedly halving the search space.** Compare the target to the middle element — if equal, found; if less, search left half; if greater, search right half. O(log n) time, O(1) space for iterative version.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you implement it correctly — the mid calculation is a classic interview pitfall
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `mid = (left + right) / 2` which overflows for large indices — correct form is `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the overflow bug and explain the correct mid calculation — this shows you know production-level details

sections.title: Halving the Search Space
sections.content: **Precondition**: array must be sorted. Initialize `left = 0`, `right = n-1`. While `left <= right`: compute `mid = left + (right - left) / 2` (overflow-safe). If `arr[mid] == target` — return mid. If `arr[mid] < target` — set `left = mid + 1` (search right half). If `arr[mid] > target` — set `right = mid - 1` (search left half). If loop ends without finding — return -1. Each iteration eliminates half the remaining elements → **O(log n)**.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Precondition: array MUST be sorted
- mid = left + (right - left) / 2 — overflow safe
- left <= right (not left < right) — handles single-element arrays
- Time: O(log n), Space: O(1) iterative / O(log n) recursive
- Java: Arrays.binarySearch() — returns negative value if not found
- Common variants: first occurrence, last occurrence, first element >= target
- log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30 — powerful for large datasets

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Binary search requires a sorted array. I use two pointers, left at 0 and right at the last index. While left is less than or equal to right, I compute the mid index as left plus right minus left divided by 2 — I always use this form rather than left plus right divided by 2 to avoid integer overflow. I compare the middle element to the target: if equal I return mid, if target is larger I set left to mid plus 1, if smaller I set right to mid minus 1. This halves the search space each iteration giving O(log n) time and O(1) space.

questions.question: How do you find the first and last occurrence of a number in a sorted array?
questions.title: First Last Occurrence Binary Search | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Modify binary search to not stop at the first match.** For first occurrence: when `arr[mid] == target`, record mid and continue searching left (`right = mid - 1`). For last occurrence: when equal, record mid and search right (`left = mid + 1`). Both O(log n).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can adapt binary search — the most common binary search variant in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Running two separate O(n) linear scans instead of recognizing it as a binary search variant
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly explain that you don't stop when you find a match — you record it and keep narrowing in the appropriate direction

sections.title: Don't Stop at the First Match
sections.content: Standard binary search returns immediately on match. To find **first occurrence**: when `arr[mid] == target`, record `result = mid` but continue narrowing left: `right = mid - 1`. The loop finds the leftmost match. For **last occurrence**: when equal, record `result = mid` but continue right: `left = mid + 1`. Run these as two separate binary search calls. Total: **O(log n)** for each.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- First occurrence: on match, save result and set right = mid - 1
- Last occurrence: on match, save result and set left = mid + 1
- Initialize result = -1; return result after loop
- Time: O(log n) for each search
- Can compute count of occurrences: last - first + 1
- This pattern extends to: first element >= target (lower bound), first element > target (upper bound)
- Java: Arrays.binarySearch returns any matching index, not necessarily first

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: This is a classic binary search variant. For first occurrence, I run a modified binary search where when I find a match I don't return immediately — instead I save the index as my current best answer and set right to mid minus 1 to keep looking in the left half. For last occurrence, same logic but I set left to mid plus 1 to keep searching right. I initialize result to negative one so I can return it if the target isn't found at all. Two calls total, each O(log n). I'd also mention this can be extended to count all occurrences by subtracting last index from first index and adding one.

questions.question: How do you search in a rotated sorted array?
questions.title: Search Rotated Sorted Array | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **One half of a rotated sorted array is always normally sorted.** At each step, identify which half is sorted. If the target falls within that sorted half, search there. Otherwise search the other half. O(log n) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to adapt a known algorithm to a modified problem — a sign of deeper algorithmic thinking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reverting to linear search O(n) or not realizing that one half is always sorted
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the key insight clearly: after computing mid, exactly one of the two halves [left..mid] or [mid..right] is always guaranteed to be sorted

sections.title: One Half is Always Sorted
sections.content: Array [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] is [0,1,2,3,4,5,6] rotated at index 4. Key insight: **after computing mid, one of the two halves is always normally sorted**. Check: if `arr[left] <= arr[mid]`, the left half is sorted. Otherwise the right half is sorted. Then check if target falls within the sorted half's range. If yes, search that half. If no, search the other half.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Standard binary search doesn't work directly on rotated arrays
- Key insight: one half is always normally sorted
- If arr[left] <= arr[mid]: left half is sorted
- Else: right half is sorted
- Check if target in sorted half's range — if yes, narrow to that half
- Time: O(log n), Space: O(1)
- Handle duplicates variant: when arr[left] == arr[mid], must do left++ to resolve ambiguity

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key observation is that in a rotated sorted array, at least one of the two halves around the midpoint is always normally sorted. I check if the left half from left to mid is sorted by comparing arr[left] to arr[mid]. If left half is sorted, I check if the target falls in that range — if yes, I search left; if no, I search right. If the right half is sorted instead, I do the same check on the right range. This way I still eliminate half the search space at each step, maintaining O(log n) time complexity.

questions.question: What is the difference between Arrays.binarySearch() and a manual binary search in Java?
questions.title: Arrays.binarySearch vs Manual Binary Search Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`Arrays.binarySearch()` is Java's built-in binary search.** It returns the index if found, or `-(insertion point) - 1` if not found. It requires the array to be sorted first. Manual binary search gives you full control — useful for variants like finding first/last occurrence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Java API knowledge alongside algorithmic understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Arrays.binarySearch returns a negative value when not found (not -1 specifically)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the negative return value formula and when you'd use the built-in vs a manual implementation

sections.title: Built-In vs Manual Control
sections.content: `Arrays.binarySearch(arr, target)` finds any matching index (not necessarily first/last occurrence). If not found, returns `-(insertionPoint) - 1` — a negative value indicating where the element would be inserted. **Must sort first**: unsorted array → undefined behavior. Manual binary search lets you customize behavior: stop on first match vs continue, return first vs last occurrence, search on custom conditions beyond equality.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Arrays.binarySearch: found → index (≥0); not found → negative value
- Not found return: -(insertionPoint) - 1
- Array must be sorted before calling — Arrays.sort() first
- Does not guarantee first or last occurrence on duplicates
- Works for int[], char[], and Object arrays with Comparator
- Manual binary search: full control for variants
- Use built-in for production code; manual for interview variants

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Arrays.binarySearch is convenient for simple existence checks and returns the index if found. If the element isn't in the array, it returns a negative value equal to negative of the insertion point minus one — so you can tell both that it's absent and where it would be inserted. The important caveats are: the array must already be sorted, and with duplicates it doesn't guarantee returning the first or last occurrence. For interview problems like finding first occurrence or searching in a rotated array, I'd write the binary search manually to have full control over the termination and adjustment logic.

questions.question: How do you find the square root of a number using binary search?
questions.title: Square Root Binary Search Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Binary search the answer space from 1 to n.** For integer square root: if `mid * mid == n` return mid; if `mid * mid < n` set left = mid + 1; else set right = mid - 1. Return right (largest mid where mid*mid <= n). O(log n) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize binary search on the answer space — not just on an existing array
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Math.sqrt() directly (trivial) or not recognizing this as a binary search problem
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the key insight: 'I'm binary searching on the answer space 1 to n, not on an array' — this shows pattern recognition

sections.title: Binary Search on the Answer Space
sections.content: Instead of searching an array, we **binary search the answer space** from 1 to n. We're looking for the largest integer x such that x*x ≤ n. `left = 1`, `right = n`. Each iteration: `mid = left + (right-left)/2`. If `mid*mid == n` — exact answer, return mid. If `mid*mid < n` — mid might be the answer but check larger: `left = mid + 1`, save `result = mid`. If `mid*mid > n` — too large: `right = mid - 1`. Return `result` (or `right`) after loop. Use `long` for `mid*mid` to avoid overflow.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Binary search on the answer space, not an array
- Condition: find largest mid where mid*mid <= n
- Use long to avoid overflow: (long)mid * mid
- Time: O(log n), Space: O(1)
- Pattern extends to: find nth root, minimum capacity problems
- Math.sqrt() uses hardware; this shows the algorithm
- 'Binary search the answer' is a key interview pattern

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key insight is that I can binary search on the answer space — from 1 to n — rather than on an array. I'm looking for the largest integer whose square is less than or equal to n. I compute mid, then check mid squared. If mid squared equals n, I return mid. If mid squared is less than n, mid could be the floor answer but there might be something larger, so I save mid as my result and search right. If mid squared exceeds n, I search left. I cast mid to long before squaring to prevent overflow. This is O(log n) and demonstrates a broader pattern of binary searching on answer ranges.

questions.question: What is the difference between finding the first and last occurrence of an element using binary search?
questions.title: Binary Search First Last Occurrence
questions.direct_answer: Finding the first occurrence continues searching left after a match; finding the last occurrence continues searching right after a match — both require not stopping at the first hit.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can adapt binary search beyond the simple 'find any match' form
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning immediately on the first match instead of narrowing the range further
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why you store the result and continue rather than returning early

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Standard binary search returns as soon as it finds the target. But when a sorted array has duplicates and you need the first or last position, you have to keep going even after a match.

For the first occurrence: when you find arr[mid] equals the target, you save mid as your current best answer and then set right to mid minus one — forcing the search to continue in the left half. You keep doing this until the search space is exhausted, and then return the saved index.

For the last occurrence: it's symmetric. When arr[mid] equals the target, save mid as the answer and set left to mid plus one — forcing the search into the right half.

Both variants run in O(log n) time just like standard binary search. The only difference is that when you get a match, instead of returning immediately, you record the position and keep narrowing in one direction.

A common way interviewers phrase this is: 'How many times does this number appear in a sorted array?' The answer is lastOccurrence minus firstOccurrence plus one — two binary searches, O(log n) total.

This pattern also shows up in finding the leftmost or rightmost position to insert a value, which is essentially Java's Arrays.binarySearch behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
content: First occurrence: on match, save mid and set right = mid - 1 (search left half)
Last occurrence: on match, save mid and set left = mid + 1 (search right half)
Both are O(log n) — same complexity as standard binary search

questions.question: Why do you use mid = left + (right - left) / 2 instead of (left + right) / 2 in binary search?
questions.title: Binary Search Mid Calculation Overflow
questions.direct_answer: left + right can overflow a 32-bit integer when both values are large; subtracting first keeps the intermediate value within bounds.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to edge cases and integer overflow awareness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using (left + right) / 2 without thinking about overflow for large arrays
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the specific overflow condition and that this matters in production systems

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
This is a classic bug that actually existed in Java's own Arrays.binarySearch implementation until it was fixed. The issue is integer overflow.

In Java, int has a maximum value of about 2.1 billion. If left and right are both large — say both are close to Integer.MAX_VALUE — then left plus right can exceed that limit and wrap around to a negative number. Dividing a negative number by 2 gives a wrong, negative index.

The safe formula left plus open-paren right minus left close-paren divided by 2 avoids this. Since right minus left is always the size of the current search window, which is at most the array length, this intermediate value can never overflow for a valid array.

In practice, for most fresher-level problems with arrays of a few thousand elements, overflow won't happen. But demonstrating that you know this formula shows the interviewer you're thinking about edge cases and production correctness, not just the happy path.

An alternative in Java is to use unsigned right shift: (left + right) >>> 1. This works because unsigned right shift treats the sign bit as a regular bit, so even if the addition overflows, the result is still the correct average. But the subtraction form is more readable and universally understood across languages.

sections.title: Key Points
content: left + right can overflow int when both are near Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2.1 billion)
Safe form: mid = left + (right - left) / 2 — intermediate never exceeds array length
Java alternative: (left + right) >>> 1 (unsigned right shift handles overflow)
This bug was present in Java's own Arrays.binarySearch before JDK fix

questions.question: Can binary search be applied to problems other than searching in sorted arrays?
questions.title: Binary Search Applications Beyond Arrays
questions.direct_answer: Yes — binary search applies to any monotonic search space: finding a minimum feasible value, searching in a rotated array, or solving optimization problems where the answer space itself is sorted.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of understanding — whether the candidate sees binary search as a pattern, not just an array operation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking binary search only applies to sorted arrays with direct element lookup
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete non-array example like finding a square root or a minimum capacity problem

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Binary search is really a strategy for any problem where the search space is monotonic — meaning if something is true at position x, it's true for all positions after x, or vice versa. You don't need a literal sorted array.

One example is computing the integer square root. The answer lies somewhere between 0 and n. You binary search on this range: if mid squared is less than or equal to n, the answer is at least mid, so you move left up. Otherwise you move right down. This converges to the floor of the square root.

Another example is finding the minimum shipping capacity for packages. Given packages of various weights and a number of days, you need the minimum capacity such that all packages can be shipped. The capacity search space is monotonic: if capacity C works, then C+1 also works. So you binary search on capacity values.

In rotated sorted arrays — like [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] — you can still use binary search by checking which half is sorted and deciding which side your target must be in.

The key question to ask yourself is: 'Is my search space ordered in some way? Can I write a condition that tells me to go left or go right?' If yes, binary search probably applies. This broader view is what separates candidates who only memorize patterns from those who understand the underlying idea.

content: Binary search applies to any monotonic decision space, not just sorted arrays
Search on answer: binary search the value range when checking feasibility is O(n)
Rotated sorted array: determine which half is sorted, then decide which half has the target
Key question: 'Does a condition split my space cleanly into go-left / go-right?'
